script.opening: (Frustrated, half-joking, rubs his hairline.) "Right doc, I'll be honest — I've spent an absolute fortune. Caffeine shampoo, biotin, a derma roller, some online kit that promised regrowth. None of it's done a thing. My hair's going the same way my dad's did and it's really getting to me. Just tell me straight: what actually works, and what's a con?"

facts.text: "It's going at the temples and the crown. Same as my dad and my grandad." "Gradual. Two years or so. No patches." Not shedding in handfuls. Will tilt his head to show the crown on camera: "There — see?"
If asked: "No, the scalp's fine" — no itch, redness, scale, pain or scarring. No recent illness, surgery, crash diet or big stress. Feels well — no tiredness, weight change or feeling hot or cold.

Caffeine shampoo, biotin tablets, a "hair vitamins" supplement, a derma roller and an online "regrowth kit" (doesn't know what was in it). About £600 over 18 months. Never tried minoxidil or finasteride.

No prescribed medicines. No steroids or bodybuilding supplements. No allergies. No past history of depression, but if asked about mood when hearing about finasteride side-effects: no previous low mood or suicidal thoughts.
If asked: has a partner, Leah; they might try for a baby "in a couple of years". Not trying now.
Sales rep — "appearance matters in my job". Non-smoker, drinks at weekends, goes to the gym.

If asked how it affects him: "Confidence, mostly. Photos, the mirror. I think I thought if I found the right product it would stop. Now I feel a bit stupid for spending so much." Checks it often: "Not hours. I'm not depressed, just fed up with it."

Frustrated but good-humoured. Wants honesty, dislikes vague answers. If dismissed ("it's only hair"), become irritated: "Easy for you to say." Ask "How long before I'd know?" and "I've read scary stuff online about the tablet" — wants a straight answer on finasteride side-effects. Ends: "That's the first straight answer I've had."

ice.ideas: "It's my dad's genes — but there must be something that works if I find the right product."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — it is knocking his confidence at work and in photos, and he feels foolish about the money wasted; he has read frightening things about finasteride online.
ice.expectations: "Just tell me straight: what works and what's a con."

cues: "It's really getting to me." — invites exploring the impact.
"Now I feel a bit stupid for spending so much." — embarrassment to acknowledge, not judge.
"I've read scary stuff online." — wants honest side-effect information.

checkpoints.text: Diagnoses androgenetic alopecia confidently from the pattern (bitemporal recession + vertex thinning) and family history, without unnecessary investigations when typical
Briefly EXCLUDES mimics — telogen effluvium, iron/thyroid (ferritin/TFTs if diffuse shedding), alopecia areata, and scarring alopecia (which needs dermatology) — with a targeted history/examination

Gives an HONEST evidence summary of what works — topical minoxidil and oral finasteride — with realistic effect size, a realistic time course (minoxidil judged after at least 6 and possibly 12 months, BAD; finasteride a year or more, SPC), the maintenance/ongoing-use caveat, and finasteride’s sexual side-effects (may persist after stopping), mood/suicidal-ideation warning (MHRA Drug Safety Update April 2024: ask about depression first), PSA lowering and teratogenicity/handling

Names clearly what is mostly MARKETING (caffeine shampoos, biotin/supplements without deficiency, derma-rollers/laser) and mentions transplant/cosmetic options neutrally — and is clear these treatments cannot be prescribed on an NHS FP10 (NHS Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA): minoxidil is bought over the counter and finasteride obtained privately
Explores the EMOTIONAL impact (identity, confidence, mood, relationships), screens low mood/body-image preoccupation, and validates the distress without trivialising or over-medicalising
Responds to his frustration and the wasted spend with empathy and respect — honest without being dismissive ("it’s only hair") and supportive of his autonomy
Sets realistic expectations and supports an informed choice (treat / cosmetic / accept), checking understanding rather than overselling a cure

Safety-nets and follows up: realistic review timeframe for any treatment trial, when to return (new patches, scarring, scalp symptoms, low mood), signposting (reliable information, counselling if distress is significant), and an honest, supportive plan — evidence and empathy, not a hard sell

worked.txt: "Let me give you the honest version you asked for. What you’ve got is male-pattern hair loss — the same gradual, patterned thinning your dad had. It’s genetic and it’s incredibly common; it’s not a sign of anything wrong with your health."

"I’ll just make sure there’s nothing else going on — any sudden shedding all over, any smooth bald patches, scalp redness or scaling? … No. Then I don’t think we need lots of tests; this is the classic pattern."

"Two things have real evidence: a solution called minoxidil you put on the scalp, and a tablet called finasteride. They slow the loss and can thicken things up a bit — but they’re slow: give the lotion at least six months, possibly a year, and the tablet a year or more to show what it can do; they work best started early, and only keep working while you use them. The tablet’s a bit more effective but can affect sex drive or function in a small number of men — about two in a hundred — occasionally even after stopping, and has been linked to low mood, so before anything else I’d ask whether you’ve ever had depression. It also lowers the PSA blood test, which matters if you ever have one. And I should be upfront: neither can be prescribed on the NHS, so the lotion is bought over the counter and the tablet comes through a private prescriber."

"And the honest bad news on the money: caffeine shampoos, biotin and most ‘growth’ supplements don’t have good evidence unless you’re actually deficient, which is rare. The rollers and laser caps are weak at best. You weren’t doing anything daft — the marketing is genuinely convincing."

"Can I ask how this is affecting you, honestly? It’s clearly more than vanity — it’s getting to you. … That matters, and you’re not being silly. Hair loss young can knock your confidence hard, and we can take that seriously too."

"There’s no wrong answer here — try a treatment, go cosmetic, or decide it’s not worth the hassle; I’ll support whatever you choose. If you try minoxidil or finasteride, take a photo now as a baseline, give it at least six months and we’ll review. And if your mood’s taking a real hit, come back — that’s worth tackling in its own right."

f.learning: Androgenetic alopecia (male-pattern hair loss) is a confident CLINICAL diagnosis — gradual patterned loss (bitemporal recession, vertex thinning) in a post-pubertal man, usually with family history and hair miniaturisation, needing little or no investigation when typical. Briefly exclude mimics: telogen effluvium (diffuse, often reversible post-stressor shedding), iron deficiency/thyroid disease (ferritin, TFTs if diffuse shedding), alopecia areata (smooth patches, exclamation-mark hairs), and SCARRING alopecia (erythema, scaling, lost follicular openings — irreversible, refer dermatology). The honest evidence: TOPICAL MINOXIDIL and ORAL FINASTERIDE are the two treatments that genuinely work — they slow loss and partially regrow but are slow (minoxidil judged after at least 6 and possibly 12 months, BAD 2016; finasteride a year or more, SPC), work best early, and only maintain benefit while continued; finasteride is more effective but carries sexual side-effects in a minority (about 2%, may persist after stopping), a depression/suicidal-ideation warning (MHRA Drug Safety Update April 2024, reinforced May 2026 — ask about mood history first, especially given his distress), lowers PSA, and is teratogenic/not for women, while minoxidil can cause irritation and initial shedding — and neither can be prescribed on an NHS FP10 (NHS Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA), so both are bought or obtained privately. Be straight that caffeine shampoos, biotin and most supplements (absent deficiency), and derma-rollers/laser, are largely marketing with little good evidence; mention transplant and cosmetic options neutrally. The real consultation, though, is the EMOTIONAL one: heavy spending and frustration signal genuine distress, as hair loss young can hit identity, confidence and mood — explore and validate the impact, screen low mood/body-image preoccupation, set realistic expectations, and support whatever informed choice he makes, neither trivialising ("it’s only hair") nor overselling a cure.

knowledge.guideline: PCDS Hair Loss: Primary Care Treatment Pathway (Nov 2024) · BAD male pattern hair loss leaflet (2016) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024 and May 2026) · finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil 5% SPCs · NHS Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA · NICE CG31
knowledge.summary: Temple recession and crown thinning with a strong family history is a clinical diagnosis of male pattern hair loss. Two treatments have evidence — topical minoxidil and oral finasteride — neither is available on an NHS prescription, and both work only while used.

points.t: Patterned loss at the temples and crown with miniaturised hairs and a family history needs no tests when typical. Check the scalp for scarring (redness, scale, loss of follicle openings) — scarring alopecia needs urgent dermatology referral (PCDS 2024).

Telogen effluvium (diffuse shedding 2–6 months after a trigger, settling over 6–9 months), alopecia areata (smooth patches, exclamation-mark hairs) and tinea capitis. FBC, ferritin and TFTs only if loss is diffuse or the picture is atypical (PCDS).

For men: 5% solution 1 ml twice daily (maximum 2 ml a day), licensed for men aged 18–49, or 5% foam twice daily per the product directions (check the SPC). Early shedding is common; judge response after at least 6 and possibly 12 months (BAD); benefit lasts only while used. Bought over the counter.

1 mg daily; 3–6 months to stabilise and a year or more to show benefit; gains reverse by 6 months and return to baseline by 9–12 months after stopping (SPC). About 2% report reduced libido or erection problems (BAD). Lowers PSA. Not for women; crushed or broken tablets should not be handled in pregnancy.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024 and 11 May 2026): ask about any history of depression or suicidal thoughts before prescribing, give the patient alert card, and stop if depression or suicidal thoughts develop; sexual effects may persist after stopping.

Finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil scalp preparations are listed in NHS Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA and cannot be prescribed on FP10. Caffeine shampoos, biotin (without deficiency) and most supplements lack good evidence; biotin can interfere with some laboratory tests. Screen for body dysmorphic disorder where preoccupation is marked (NICE CG31).

model.text: Hi Jordan, I’m Dr Lee. That sounds like a lot of money and hope spent on things that haven’t worked. I’ll give you the honest version, I promise. First, can you tell me what you’ve noticed and how it’s been affecting you?
model.why: Acknowledges frustration and commits to honesty before gathering data

model.text: It’s going at the temples and the crown. Same as my dad and my grandad. And it’s really getting to me — I check it all the time.
Thanks. I’d like to check a few things to be sure it’s what it looks like, then go through what really works, what doesn’t, and what fits you. Okay?
Yeah, go for it.
Is it a gradual thinning in those areas, or have you noticed hair coming out in handfuls, or smooth bald patches anywhere?
model.why: Distinguishes patterned loss from telogen effluvium and alopecia areata

model.text: Gradual. Two years or so. No patches.
Any itching, soreness, redness or flaking on the scalp?
model.why: Screens for scarring alopecia and tinea capitis

model.text: No, the scalp’s fine.
Any big illness, operation, crash diet or very stressful time in the months before it started? And any tiredness, weight change or feeling the cold?
model.why: Screens for triggers of shedding and thyroid or iron problems

model.text: Nothing like that.
Could you show me the front and crown on the camera, in good light?
model.why: Uses video to confirm the pattern

model.text: (Tilts head.) There — see?

I can see recession at the temples and thinning at the crown, and your scalp looks healthy. With your family history, this is male pattern hair loss — genes and hormones, not something you’ve done wrong.
model.why: Confident clinical diagnosis without unnecessary tests

model.text: You said it’s really getting to you and you check it all the time. Can you tell me more about how it’s affecting you?
Confidence, mostly. Photos, the mirror. I think I thought if I found the right product it would stop. Now I feel a bit stupid for spending so much.

You’re not stupid — those products are marketed very cleverly, and hair matters to how people see themselves. How has your mood been generally? Does it ever take up hours of your day or stop you going out?
model.why: Validates and screens low mood and body dysmorphic concern

model.text: Not hours. I’m not depressed, just fed up with it.

Here’s the straight answer. Two treatments have good evidence. Minoxidil is a lotion or foam you use twice a day. Finasteride is a daily tablet. Both slow the loss and can bring some regrowth, especially at the crown. Neither brings it all back.
How long before I’d know?

Minoxidil often causes a bit of extra shedding at first, and you need at least six months, possibly a year, to judge it. Finasteride takes a year or more. And both only work while you use them — stop, and within about a year you’re back to where you would have been.
model.why: Realistic time course and ongoing-use caveat

model.text: Right. And the tablet — I’ve read scary stuff online.

It’s fair to ask. A small number of men get reduced sex drive or erection problems, and occasionally these carry on after stopping. The medicines regulator also warns about low mood and suicidal thoughts, so before anyone prescribes it they should ask about your mental health. Has there been any depression in the past?
model.why: MHRA 2024 and 2026 warnings, with the required mood history

model.text: Not that I know of.

Thanks. And the shampoos, biotin and kits — there’s little good evidence they help unless you’re actually deficient. Neither minoxidil nor finasteride can be prescribed on the NHS for this, so they’re bought from a pharmacy or privately. A transplant is also possible privately, at real cost.
model.why: Names the marketing honestly and explains NHS access

model.text: So the options are: try minoxidil, consider finasteride through a pharmacy or private prescriber, look at cosmetic options, or decide not to treat. All are reasonable. What feels right to you?
Probably minoxidil first. Stop wasting money on the other stuff.

That sounds sensible. Take photos now in the same light, so in six months you can compare fairly. If you notice patches, a sore or red scalp, or your mood dropping — especially if you start finasteride — come back. And if it starts taking over your day, we can talk about support for that too.
model.why: Review point, return triggers and mood safety-net

model.text: Okay. That’s the first straight answer I’ve had.
Just so I know it landed, what will you tell a mate who asks what works?
Minoxidil or finasteride, give it a year, keep using it — and the shampoos are a con.
Spot on. I’ll send you some reliable reading, and we can review in six months if you’d like.
model.why: Closes with signposting and optional review

social.t: Money spent on unproven products can bring shame as well as frustration. Naming the marketing, not the man, keeps trust.
Hair loss in young men can affect confidence, dating, work and photos. Ask about impact; most need validation and information, a few need support for mood or body dysmorphic concern.

legal.t: NHS Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA lists finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil scalp preparations as not prescribable on FP10. Advice remains NHS care; supply is by pharmacy or private prescription.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024, May 2026): patient alert card for finasteride; ask about depression and suicidal thoughts before prescribing; report suspected reactions via the Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): give honest, balanced information. Advise that online prescribers should take a mood history and give the MHRA warnings before supplying finasteride.
No treatment is a legitimate informed choice. GMC decision-making and consent guidance (2020) applies to cosmetic as well as medical decisions.

community.t: BAD patient leaflet on male pattern hair loss; Alopecia UK for peer support.
NHS Talking Therapies self-referral if low mood or body-image distress is significant.

redFlags: Red, scaly or sore scalp with loss of follicle openings → possible scarring alopecia; urgent dermatology referral (PCDS 2024)
Sudden smooth patches or diffuse shedding → reconsider alopecia areata or telogen effluvium
Low mood, suicidal thoughts or hours of preoccupation → assess mental health; no finasteride without a mood history
psychosocial: Mood and any past depression, before discussing finasteride
ice: Idea: the right product exists and he just hasn’t found it
Concern: losing his hair young, like his father; confidence
Expectation: a straight answer on what works and what is a con

playbook.diagnosis: “This is male pattern hair loss — the pattern and your family history fit exactly, and your scalp is healthy. It’s genes and hormones, not something you caused.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your hair follicles are slowly shrinking under the effect of a hormone, so each new hair grows thinner and shorter. The treatments that work slow that shrinking; they can’t undo all of it.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked for the straight answer, so here it is — and I’m sorry you’ve spent so much on things that were never going to work.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the distress, screen mood proportionately, and present no treatment and cosmetic options as legitimate choices.
sharedPlan: Minoxidil 5% solution 1 ml twice daily (maximum 2 ml a day) or 5% foam twice daily per product directions; expect early shedding; judge at 6–12 months; continue to keep benefit
Finasteride 1 mg only after a mood history and the MHRA warnings; sexual side effects may persist; lowers PSA; private or pharmacy supply
Stop spending on unproven products; baseline photos; consider cosmetic options or transplant privately if wanted
safetyNet: Return for patches, a red or sore scalp, or low mood (stop finasteride and seek help if mood changes)
Review at about six months with comparison photos

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by being either dismissive or salesy. He asked for honesty — the marks go to the candidate who gives it with warmth.

items.why: Trivialises real distress and misses the emotional task.
items.fix: Ask how it affects him and reflect it back before giving facts.

items.fail: Ordering a full blood screen for typical patterned loss.
items.why: Male pattern hair loss is a clinical diagnosis; tests add cost and delay when the picture is typical (PCDS 2024).
items.fix: Brief screen for mimics; bloods only if diffuse shedding or atypical features.

items.fail: Recommending finasteride without asking about mood.
items.why: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024 and May 2026) asks prescribers to ask about depression and suicidal thoughts first.
items.fix: Take a mood history and name the sexual and mood warnings before any recommendation.

items.why: Unrealistic timelines lead to stopping early. BAD advises at least six and possibly twelve months for minoxidil; finasteride needs a year or more.
items.fix: Give realistic timeframes and suggest baseline photos.

items.fail: Leaving out NHS access, so he expects a prescription.
items.why: Finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil scalp preparations are in Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA.
items.fix: Explain supply honestly and what to check with online providers.

items.fail: No choice offered and no review point.
items.why: Shared decision-making and follow-up are both marked.
items.fix: Lay out options including no treatment; agree review at about six months.

That sounds sensible. Take photos now in the same light, so in six months you can compare fairly. If you notice patches, a sore or red scalp, or your mood dropping — especially if you start finasteride — come back. And if it starts taking over your day, we can talk about support for that too.
SCA_MODELS.why: Review point, return triggers and mood safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s the first straight answer I’ve had.
Just so I know it landed, what will you tell a mate who asks what works?
Minoxidil or finasteride, give it a year, keep using it — and the shampoos are a con.
Spot on. I’ll send you some reliable reading, and we can review in six months if you’d like.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with signposting and optional review

SCA_STEM.name: Jordan Ashby
meds: No prescribed medication; self-bought caffeine shampoo, biotin and ‘thickening’ supplements
SCA_STEM.recent: Two years of receding at the temples and thinning at the crown. Father and grandfather bald early. Has tried caffeine shampoo, biotin, supplements, a derma roller and an online regrowth kit without benefit.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: “What actually works for my hair?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: PCDS Hair Loss: Primary Care Treatment Pathway (Nov 2024) · BAD male pattern hair loss leaflet (2016) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024 and May 2026) · finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil 5% SPCs · NHS Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA · NICE CG31
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Temple recession and crown thinning with a strong family history is a clinical diagnosis of male pattern hair loss. Two treatments have evidence — topical minoxidil and oral finasteride — neither is available on an NHS prescription, and both work only while used.

points.t: Patterned loss at the temples and crown with miniaturised hairs and a family history needs no tests when typical. Check the scalp for scarring (redness, scale, loss of follicle openings) — scarring alopecia needs urgent dermatology referral (PCDS 2024).

Telogen effluvium (diffuse shedding 2–6 months after a trigger, settling over 6–9 months), alopecia areata (smooth patches, exclamation-mark hairs) and tinea capitis. FBC, ferritin and TFTs only if loss is diffuse or the picture is atypical (PCDS).

For men: 5% solution 1 ml twice daily (maximum 2 ml a day), licensed for men aged 18–49, or 5% foam twice daily per the product directions (check the SPC). Early shedding is common; judge response after at least 6 and possibly 12 months (BAD); benefit lasts only while used. Bought over the counter.

1 mg daily; 3–6 months to stabilise and a year or more to show benefit; gains reverse by 6 months and return to baseline by 9–12 months after stopping (SPC). About 2% report reduced libido or erection problems (BAD). Lowers PSA. Not for women; crushed or broken tablets should not be handled in pregnancy.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024 and 11 May 2026): ask about any history of depression or suicidal thoughts before prescribing, give the patient alert card, and stop if depression or suicidal thoughts develop; sexual effects may persist after stopping.

Finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil scalp preparations are listed in NHS Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA and cannot be prescribed on FP10. Caffeine shampoos, biotin (without deficiency) and most supplements lack good evidence; biotin can interfere with some laboratory tests. Screen for body dysmorphic disorder where preoccupation is marked (NICE CG31).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged the money and frustration; let him say how it affects him before narrowing.
Explored confidence, mirror-checking and photos; the cost of past products; mood; his wish for honesty.
Followed ‘it’s really getting to me’ and ‘I feel stupid’; screened for body dysmorphic concern without over-medicalising.
Idea: the right product exists. Concern: confidence and following his father’s pattern. Expectation: a straight answer.
Inspected scalp by video in good light; no bloods needed for typical pattern; FBC, ferritin, TFTs only if diffuse or atypical.
Male pattern hair loss vs telogen effluvium, alopecia areata, tinea capitis and scarring alopecia.
Asked about scalp redness, soreness or scale (scarring alopecia → urgent dermatology) and about patches; screened mood before any finasteride.
Stated male pattern hair loss confidently and explained it in plain words.

Honest options: minoxidil (5% solution 1 ml or 5% foam, twice daily; judge at 6–12 months), finasteride 1 mg (MHRA mood and sexual warnings), cosmetic, transplant, or no treatment; NHS access explained.
Addressed mood and self-image; noted finasteride lowers PSA; not for women and pregnancy handling caution.
Baseline photos; review at about six months; return for patches, scalp symptoms or low mood; reliable information given.

social.t: Money spent on unproven products can bring shame as well as frustration. Naming the marketing, not the man, keeps trust.
Hair loss in young men can affect confidence, dating, work and photos. Ask about impact; most need validation and information, a few need support for mood or body dysmorphic concern.

legal.t: NHS Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA lists finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil scalp preparations as not prescribable on FP10. Advice remains NHS care; supply is by pharmacy or private prescription.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024, May 2026): patient alert card for finasteride; ask about depression and suicidal thoughts before prescribing; report suspected reactions via the Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): give honest, balanced information. Advise that online prescribers should take a mood history and give the MHRA warnings before supplying finasteride.
No treatment is a legitimate informed choice. GMC decision-making and consent guidance (2020) applies to cosmetic as well as medical decisions.

community.t: BAD patient leaflet on male pattern hair loss; Alopecia UK for peer support.
NHS Talking Therapies self-referral if low mood or body-image distress is significant.

redFlags: Red, scaly or sore scalp with loss of follicle openings → possible scarring alopecia; urgent dermatology referral (PCDS 2024)
Sudden smooth patches or diffuse shedding → reconsider alopecia areata or telogen effluvium
Low mood, suicidal thoughts or hours of preoccupation → assess mental health; no finasteride without a mood history
psychosocial: Mood and any past depression, before discussing finasteride
ice: Idea: the right product exists and he just hasn’t found it
Concern: losing his hair young, like his father; confidence
Expectation: a straight answer on what works and what is a con

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is male pattern hair loss — the pattern and your family history fit exactly, and your scalp is healthy. It’s genes and hormones, not something you caused.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your hair follicles are slowly shrinking under the effect of a hormone, so each new hair grows thinner and shorter. The treatments that work slow that shrinking; they can’t undo all of it.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked for the straight answer, so here it is — and I’m sorry you’ve spent so much on things that were never going to work.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the distress, screen mood proportionately, and present no treatment and cosmetic options as legitimate choices.
sharedPlan: Minoxidil 5% solution 1 ml twice daily (maximum 2 ml a day) or 5% foam twice daily per product directions; expect early shedding; judge at 6–12 months; continue to keep benefit
Finasteride 1 mg only after a mood history and the MHRA warnings; sexual side effects may persist; lowers PSA; private or pharmacy supply
Stop spending on unproven products; baseline photos; consider cosmetic options or transplant privately if wanted
safetyNet: Return for patches, a red or sore scalp, or low mood (stop finasteride and seek help if mood changes)
Review at about six months with comparison photos

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by being either dismissive or salesy. He asked for honesty — the marks go to the candidate who gives it with warmth.

items.why: Trivialises real distress and misses the emotional task.
items.fix: Ask how it affects him and reflect it back before giving facts.

items.fail: Ordering a full blood screen for typical patterned loss.
items.why: Male pattern hair loss is a clinical diagnosis; tests add cost and delay when the picture is typical (PCDS 2024).
items.fix: Brief screen for mimics; bloods only if diffuse shedding or atypical features.

items.fail: Recommending finasteride without asking about mood.
items.why: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024 and May 2026) asks prescribers to ask about depression and suicidal thoughts first.
items.fix: Take a mood history and name the sexual and mood warnings before any recommendation.

items.why: Unrealistic timelines lead to stopping early. BAD advises at least six and possibly twelve months for minoxidil; finasteride needs a year or more.
items.fix: Give realistic timeframes and suggest baseline photos.

items.fail: Leaving out NHS access, so he expects a prescription.
items.why: Finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil scalp preparations are in Drug Tariff Part XVIIIA.
items.fix: Explain supply honestly and what to check with online providers.

items.fail: No choice offered and no review point.
items.why: Shared decision-making and follow-up are both marked.
items.fix: Lay out options including no treatment; agree review at about six months.
